'''Lisa Perez Jackson'''<ref name="Tulane"/>  (born February 8, 1962) is an American [[chemical engineer]] who served as the [[Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency|administrator]] of the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) from 2009 to 2013. She was the first [[African American]] to hold that position.

In 2002, Jackson joined the [[New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection]] as the assistant commissioner of compliance and enforcement and assistant commissioner for land use management. [[Governor of New Jersey|New Jersey governor]] [[Jon Corzine]] appointed Jackson the state's commissioner of environmental protection in 2006. Jackson also briefly served as Corzine's [[Chief of Staff|chief of staff]] in late 2008.

On December 15, 2008, President-elect [[Barack Obama]] nominated Jackson to serve as administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency; she was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] on January 23, 2009, and took office that same day.  During her tenure as EPA administrator, Jackson oversaw the development of stricter fuel efficiency standards and the EPA's response to the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill]]; authorized the recognition of [[carbon dioxide]] as a public health threat, granting the EPA authority to set new [[regulation of greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act]]; and proposed amending the [[National Ambient Air Quality Standards]] to set stricter smog pollution limits. In December 2012, Jackson announced she would step down as EPA administrator effective February 15, 2013; she was succeeded by Deputy Administrator [[Bob Perciasepe]], who served as acting administrator until the Senate confirmed [[Gina McCarthy]] as a permanent successor on July 18, 2013.

==Early life, education and family==
Jackson was born in [[Philadelphia]] and was adopted two weeks after her birth by Benjamin and Marie Perez.<ref name="Tulane">{{cite web|url=https://exhibits.tulane.edu/exhibit/tulanewomen/academicwomen/lisa-perez-jackson/|title=Lisa Perez Jackson|publisher=Tulane University Howard-Tilton Memorial Library|access-date=December 21, 2020}}</ref> She grew up in [[Pontchartrain Park]], a predominantly [[African-American]] middle-class neighborhood of [[New Orleans, Louisiana]].<ref>{{cite news|title=New Orleans community rises and shines | publisher=[[CNN]]|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2010/OPINION/08/20/jackson.pontchartrain.park/|author=Jackson, Lisa|date=August 20, 2010}}</ref>  In 1979, Jackson graduated as [[valedictorian]] from [[St. Mary's Dominican High School]] in New Orleans.<ref name=NJDEP>Biographical information. [https://web.archive.org/web/20070927183737/http://www.state.nj.us/dep/commissioner/bio.html "About Commissioner Lisa P. Jackson"], New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection, accessed December 12, 2008.</ref>{{failed verification|date=October 2020}}<ref name=NOLALPJ>Biographical information. [https://www.nola.com/news/obama-taps-new-orleans-native-lisa-jackson-to-lead-environmental-protection-agency/article_faf676ec-5600-5d7e-9190-230a1718cd63.html "Obama taps New Orleans native Lisa Jackson to lead Environmental Protection Agency"]</ref> Due to her exceptional performance in mathematics, she received a scholarship from the National Consortium for Graduate Degrees for Minorities in Engineering & Science, which allowed her to gain early exposure to a college environment.<ref name="cen-prof">{{cite news | url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/88/8819cover.html | title=Lisa P. Jackson | author=Hoque, Cheryl | magazine=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] | date=May 10, 2010 }}</ref>

She attended [[Tulane University]] with a scholarship from [[Shell Oil Company]].<ref name="cen-prof"/>  Jackson was also named a [[National Merit Scholarship Program|National Merit Scholar]]. A dean at the [[Tulane University School of Science and Engineering|Tulane School of Engineering]] inspired her to pursue engineering, and she graduated ''[[summa cum laude]]'' with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[chemical engineering]] in 1983.<ref name="cen-prof"/>  Jackson went on to earn a [[Master of Science]] in chemical engineering from [[Princeton University]] in 1986.

Jackson's mother was living in New Orleans at the time [[Hurricane Katrina]] flooded the city in 2005, and Jackson drove her out of the city.<ref name="tilove">Tilove, Jonathan. [http://www.nola.com/news/index.ssf/2008/12/obama_taps_no_graduate_for_epa.html  "Obama taps New Orleans native Lisa Jackson to lead Environmental Protection Agency"]. ''[[The Times-Picayune]]'', December 15, 2009, retrieved January 23, 2009</ref> Jackson is married to Kenneth Jackson and is the mother of two children.<ref name=NJDEP />

Jackson has been a resident of [[East Windsor Township, New Jersey]], along with her husband and two sons.<ref>Kocieniewski, David. [https://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/11/us/politics/11web-jackson.html "The New Team: Lisa P. Jackson"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', December 11, 2008. Accessed December 3, 2012. "She lives with her husband, Kenny Jackson, and their two sons in East Windsor, N.J."</ref>

On July 13, 2013, she was initiated into [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority as an honorary member during the organization's Centennial Celebration in Washington, DC.

==Early EPA and DEP career==
As a child, Jackson did not feel any particular affinity for the outdoors, but she became interested in environmental matters following the national and international coverage of the [[Love Canal#Love Canal disaster|Love Canal Disaster]].<ref name="cen-prof"/>  Prior to the EPA, she spent a year and a half working at [[Clean Sites]], a nonprofit advocating for accelerated cleanup of contaminated areas.<ref name="cen-prof"/>

In 1987, Jackson joined the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) at its headquarters in [[Washington, D.C.]], as a staff-level engineer.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://yosemite.epa.gov/opa/admpress.nsf/8d49f7ad4bbcf4ef852573590040b7f6/dbce2367cd5570b785257a8b00779a07!OpenDocument | archive-url=https://archive.today/20130308165606/http://yosemite.epa.gov/opa/admpress.nsf/8d49f7ad4bbcf4ef852573590040b7f6/dbce2367cd5570b785257a8b00779a07!OpenDocument | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 8, 2013 | title =Administrator Lisa P. Jackson, Remarks at the Water Environment Federation's Technical Exhibition and Conference, As Prepared | publisher =epa.gov | date =October 1, 2012}}</ref>  She then moved to the agency's regional office in [[New York City]].  During her tenure at EPA, Jackson worked in the federal [[Superfund]] site remediation program, developing numerous hazardous waste cleanup regulations and directing multi-million dollar hazardous waste cleanup projects throughout central [[New Jersey]]. She later served as deputy director and acting director of the region's enforcement division.<ref name=NJDEP/>

After 16 years with EPA, Jackson joined the [[New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection]] (DEP) in March 2002 as assistant commissioner of compliance and enforcement.  She served as the assistant commissioner for land use management during 2005. Jackson headed numerous programs, including land use regulation, water supply, geological survey, water monitoring and standards, and watershed management. She focused on developing a system of incentives for stimulating what was in her opinion the right growth in the right places. Under her leadership, the state Department of Environmental Protection developed regulatory standards for implementing the landmark [[Highlands Water Protection and Planning Act]].

==New Jersey commissioner of environmental protection==
[[Jon Corzine]], [[Governor of New Jersey]], nominated her to serve as commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection. Serving in that position, Jackson led a staff of 2,990 responsible for protecting and improving New Jersey's land, air, and water environment. In addition to overseeing environmental programs for the state, as commissioner, Jackson oversaw state parks and beaches, fish and wildlife programs and historic preservation. As commissioner in July 2006, she had to shut down all state parks and beaches due to the state governmental shutdown in relation to the state budget delay.

As the state's chief environmental enforcer, Jackson led compliance sweeps in [[Camden, New Jersey|Camden]] and [[Paterson, New Jersey|Paterson]], two largely working-class cities in which people of color formed the majority of the population and where the effects of pollution on public health had long been neglected. She launched the environmental initiative following multicultural outreach efforts to inform and involve community residents and businesses. Working with county officials, [[New Jersey State Police]] and the federal Environmental Protection Agency, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection then mobilized more than 70 inspectors to conduct upward of 1,000 compliance investigations in the two cities, the first of a series of enforcement sweeps.<ref name=NJDEP/>

The online environmental magazine [[Grist (magazine)|''Grist'']] interviewed several New Jersey environmental activists and reported that opinion about Jackson was divided: "The split seems to be between those who work on energy and climate policy in the state's capital [who were supportive of Jackson] and those who work on toxic cleanups at the local level [who were critical of her]."<ref>{{cite web|title=The Lisa of our concerns |author=Kate Sheppard |url=http://gristmill.grist.org/story/2009/1/5/8314/64771 |date=2009-01-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123125341/http://gristmill.grist.org/story/2009/1/5/8314/64771 |archive-date=January 23, 2009 }}</ref>

==Chief of staff to the governor of New Jersey==
On October 24, 2008, Corzine announced that Jackson would take over as his chief of staff, effective December 1, 2008, succeeding [[Bradley Abelow]].<ref name="pressreleasegovnj">Press Release. [http://www.nj.gov/governor/news/news/2008/approved/20081024b.html "Governor Corzine Names New Chief of Staff"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081028120321/http://www.nj.gov/governor/news/news/2008/approved/20081024b.html |date=2008-10-28 }},  New Jersey government official web site, October 24, 2008, accessed October 27, 2008.</ref>  As Chief of Staff Jackson would have served as Corzine's top advisor and chief political liaison to the [[New Jersey State Legislature|State Legislature]]. However, Jackson was tapped by President [[Barack Obama]] to become administrator of the EPA just days after she became Corzine's chief of staff and resigned on December 15, 2008.<ref>[http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2008/12/obama_picks_nj_official_to_lea.html Obama picks N.J. official to lead environmental agency], ''The Star Ledger'', 2008-12-10</ref>

==EPA administrator==
[[File:US Navy 100825-N-5549O-088 Secretary of the Navy (SECNAV) the Honorable Ray Mabus, center, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lisa Jackson, left, and Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley answer questions from the media.jpg|thumb|270px|Jackson with [[United States Secretary of the Navy|Secretary of the Navy]] [[Ray Mabus]] (center), and [[Governor of Maryland|Maryland Governor]] [[Martin O'Malley]] (right)]]
On December 15, 2008, then President-elect [[Barack Obama]] officially designated Jackson as the nominee for [[Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency|Administrator]] of the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]].<ref name="heininger">Heininger, Claire,  Margolin, Josh. [http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2008/12/obama_picks_nj_official_to_lea.html "Obama picks N.J. official to lead environmental agency"], NJ.com,  December 10, 2008.</ref>  She was confirmed by voice vote in the [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] on January 22, 2009.<ref>[http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/01/senate_confirms_lisa_jackson_a.html "Senate confirms Lisa Jackson as EPA administrator"], January 23, 2009. [[The Star-Ledger]], January 23, 2009, retrieved January 23, 2009.</ref>  Jackson is the first [[African American]] to serve as EPA administrator,<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/12/28/science/earth/lisa-p-jackson-of-epa-to-step-down.html | title=E.P.A. Chief Set to Leave; Term Fell Shy of Early Hope | newspaper=The New York Times | date=27 December 2012 | last1=Broder | first1=John M. }}</ref> along with being the fourth woman and second New Jerseyan to hold the position.<ref name=nytimeskocieniewski>Kocieniewski, David.[https://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/11/us/politics/11web-jackson.html  "The New Team Lisa P. Jackson"], [[The New York Times]], December 11, 2008, retrieved December 16, 2008.</ref>  Her deputy administrator was [[Bob Perciasepe]], and additionally she had three associate, twelve assistant, and ten regional administrators overseeing some 17,000 agency employees.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/leadership.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120730050815/http://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/leadership.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 30, 2012 |title=Current Leadership &#124; About EPA &#124; US EPA |publisher=Epa.gov |date=2010-11-17 |access-date=2011-04-17}}</ref>

By the EPA's own statements, Administrator Jackson pledged to focus on core issues of protecting air and water quality, preventing exposure to toxic contamination in U.S. communities, and reducing greenhouse gases. She pledged that all of the agency's efforts would follow the best science, adhere to the rule of law, and be implemented with unparalleled transparency.  By the same statements, she made it a priority to focus on vulnerable groups – including children, the elderly, and low-income communities – that are particularly susceptible to environmental and health threats. She promised that all stakeholders will be heard in the decision-making process.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/administrator.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120730154315/http://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/administrator.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 30, 2012 |title=About the EPA Administrator &#124; About EPA &#124; US EPA |publisher=Epa.gov |date=2010-11-17 |access-date=2011-04-17}}</ref>

She became the first EPA administrator to focus on reforming the [[Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976]], which regulates the introduction of new or already existing chemicals.<ref name="cen-prof"/>  Indeed, she has called this the issue "closest to my heart ... The law and the structure of the law in no way is modern enough or has enough teeth."<ref name="cen-prof"/>

On December 8, 2009, Jackson said in a written statement that the finding, which declares carbon dioxide and five other greenhouse gases a threat to public health, marks the start of a U.S. campaign to tackle greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB126020179812780059 | title =EPA Calls Greenhouse Gases a Public Threat | newspaper =[[Wall Street Journal]] |author1=Jeffrey Ball |author2=Charles Forelle |author3=Ian Talley | date =December 7, 2009}}</ref>

[[File:Obama-venice-la.jpg|thumb|270px|left|Jackson at a 2010 briefing on the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill]] at the [[United States Coast Guard|Coast Guard]] Station Venice in [[Venice, Louisiana]]]]
After the [[Deepwater Horizon drilling rig explosion]], the [[Obama administration]] ordered the EPA, the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]] and the [[United States Department of the Interior|Department of Interior]] to coordinate federal emergency response efforts.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/blog/2010/05/01/response-oil-spill-5110 | title =The Response to the Oil Spill: 5/1/10 | date =May 1, 2010 | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | access-date =December 29, 2012 }}</ref> Jackson's agency oversaw environmental and public health concerns during the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill]], including air and water monitoring and assessing aquatic life and other environmental destruction.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/deepwater-bp-oil-spill | work=[[whitehouse.gov]] | title =Deepwater BP Oil Spill | via=[[NARA|National Archives]] | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> Jackson authorized and defended [[British Petroleum|BP]]'s choice to use the dispersant [[Corexit]] to combat the 210 million gallons of oil spilled in the [[Gulf of Mexico]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.epa.gov/ocir/hearings/testimony/111_2009_2010/2010_0518_lpj.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100618081344/http://www.epa.gov/ocir/hearings/testimony/111_2009_2010/2010_0518_lpj.pdf | url-status=dead | archive-date=June 18, 2010 | title=Testimony of Lisa P. Jackson Administrator U.S. Environmental Protection Agency before the Committee on Environment and Public Works United States Senate | publisher=epa.gov | date=May 18, 2010 | access-date=December 29, 2012}}</ref> The use of Corexit was criticized because it's more toxic and less effective than other EPA approved dispersants,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/05/13/business/energy-environment/13greenwire-less-toxic-dispersants-lose-out-in-bp-oil-spil-81183.html?_r=0 | title=Less Toxic Dispersants Lose out in BP Oil Spill Cleanup | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=May 13, 2010 | access-date=December 29, 2012 | first=Paul | last=Quinlan}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.mcclatchydc.com/2010/05/06/93696/researchers-worry-about-oil-dispersants.html | title =Researchers worry about oil dispersants' impact, too | publisher = mcclatchydc.com | date =May 6, 2012 | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> which later studies showed that Corexit had major effects on the aquatic life's food chain in the Gulf of Mexico.<ref>{{cite web | url= http://www.nola.com/news/gulf-oil-spill/index.ssf/2012/07/bp_oil_spill_dispersants_may_h.html | title =BP oil spill dispersants may have hurt Gulf of Mexico food chain, study finds | publisher =nola.com | date =July 31, 2012 | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> While testifying before the [[United States Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies|Senate Appropriations Subcommittee]], Jackson called the use of dispersants an "environmental tradeoff", and that "We know dispersants are generally less toxic than the oils they break down."<ref>{{cite web | url=http://yosemite.epa.gov/opa/admpress.nsf/0/571400992A5345A58525776100509550 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20130213180545/http://yosemite.epa.gov/opa/admpress.nsf/0/571400992A5345A58525776100509550 | url-status=dead | archive-date=February 13, 2013 | title =Statement of Lisa P. Jackson Administrator, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency / Legislative Hearing on Use of Dispersants in BP Oil Spill / Senate Committee on Appropriations: Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies | publisher =yosemite.epa.gov | date =July 15, 2010 | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> Jackson's agency faced a lawsuit in response of the spill from health and environmental groups for not setting adequate guidelines on how and where dispersants can be used safely.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nola.com/news/gulf-oil-spill/index.ssf/2012/08/environmental_group_sues_epa_o.html| title =Environmental group sues EPA over dispersants used during Gulf oil spill| publisher = nola.com| date =August 7, 2012| access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> Jackson was designated by President Obama to serve as chair on the [[Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Task Force]], a federal effort to restore damages and preserve the ecosystem in the Gulf of Mexico.<ref>{{cite web| url =http://www.restorethegulf.gov/task-force/about-task-force/about-task-force| title =About the Task Force| publisher =restorethegulf.gov| access-date =December 29, 2012| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20110319170058/http://www.restorethegulf.gov/task-force/about-task-force/about-task-force| archive-date =March 19, 2011}}</ref>

In 2011, Jackson laid out a plan for stricter limits on the [[National Ambient Air Quality Standards]].<ref>{{cite web | url= http://yosemite.epa.gov/sab/sabproduct.nsf/F08BEB48C1139E2A8525785E006909AC/$File/EPA-CASAC-11-004-unsigned+.pdf | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111018035819/http://yosemite.epa.gov/sab/sabproduct.nsf/F08BEB48C1139E2A8525785E006909AC/$File/EPA-CASAC-11-004-unsigned+.pdf | url-status= dead | archive-date= October 18, 2011 | title =Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee (CASAC) Response to Charge Questions on the Reconsideration of the 2008 Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards | publisher = yosemite.epa.gov | date =March 30, 2011 | access-date = December 28, 2012}}</ref> The plan was based on adopting a 2007 recommendation from the EPA's science advisory board to set the NAAQS no higher than 70 parts per billion and no lower than 64 parts per billion,<ref>{{cite web | url=http://yosemite.epa.gov/sab/sabproduct.nsf/FE915E916333D776852572AC007397B5/$File/casac-07-002.pdf | title =Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee's (CASAC) Review of the Agency's Final Ozone Staff Paper | publisher = yosemite.epa.gov | date = March 26, 2007 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}{{dead link|date=July 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> though it was later set to 75 parts per billion in 2008.<ref>{{cite news | url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/story/2008/03/12/ST2008031203746.html | title = EPA Tightens Pollution Standards | work = washingtonpost.com| date = March 13, 2008 | access-date =December 28, 2012 | first=Juliet | last=Eilperin}}</ref> Jackson met opposition to the smog standards proposal from economic advisors within Obama's administration, along with his [[White House Chief of Staff|chief of staff]] [[William M. Daley|William Daley]] and [[Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs|regulatory affairs administrator]] [[Cass Sunstein]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/17/science/earth/policy-and-politics-collide-as-obama-enters-campaign-mode.html?pagewanted=all | title =Re-election Strategy Is Tied to a Shift on Smog | work = [[The New York Times]] | date = November 16, 2011 | access-date =December 28, 2012 | first=John M. | last=Broder}}</ref> After recommending the plan to President Obama, he conclusively rejected the proposal saying that "Ultimately, I did not support asking state and local governments to begin implementing a new standard that will soon be reconsidered."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/obama-pulls-back-proposed-smog-standards-in-victory-for-business/2011/09/02/gIQAisTiwJ_story.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121209202614/http://articles.washingtonpost.com/2011-09-02/national/35274851_1_ground-level-ozone-burdens-and-regulatory-uncertainty-smog-standards | url-status=live | archive-date=December 9, 2012 | title =Obama pulls back proposed smog standards in victory for business | work = washingtonpost.com | date =September 2, 2011 | access-date = December 28, 2012 | first=Juliet | last=Eilperin}}</ref> His decision was met with anger from environmentalists and a lawsuit from environmental and health associations, with calls and speculation on whether Administrator Jackson would resign in protest.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-pollution-suit-obama-idUSTRE79A62T20111011 | title = Greens sue Obama administration over axed smog rule | publisher = reuters.com | date =October 11, 2011| access-date = December 28, 2012 | first=Timothy | last=Gardner}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.politico.com/story/2011/09/spurned-on-smog-will-epa-head-go-062778 | title = Spurned on smog, Lisa Jackson has a choice to make | publisher = politico.com | date =September 6, 2011 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}</ref> Jackson later announced that she would stay with the EPA, "respected President Obama's decision" and that her Agency would "aggressively implement" the curtailed version of the ozone standards.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nationaljournal.com/energy/epa-chief-respected-obama-smog-decision-20110922 | title =EPA Chief 'Respected' Obama Smog Decision | work = nationaljournal.com | date =September 22, 2012 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}</ref>

[[File:Bolden & Jackson sign a Memorandum of Agreement.jpg|thumb|270px|[[NASA]] administrator [[Charles F. Bolden, Jr.|Charles Bolden]] and Jackson sign an agreement in 2010 to continue collaboration between the two agencies.]]

Media outlets and industry figures often refer to Jackson's testimony during a May 2011 Senate Hearing Committee that she is not aware of any cases where [[hydraulic fracturing]] itself has contaminated water.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://epw.senate.gov/public/index.cfm?FuseAction=PressRoom.PressReleases&ContentRecord_id=23EB85DD-802A-23AD-43F9-DA281B2CD287|publisher=U.S. Senate |title=Pathways To Energy Independence: Hydraulic Fracturing And Other New Technologies  |date=May 6, 2011}}</ref> A 1987 EPA report and reports released since May 2011, however, have identified hydraulic fracturing as the likely source of water contamination in several cases.<ref name="Phillips 2011">{{cite web |url=http://stateimpact.npr.org/pennsylvania/2011/12/08/epa-blames-fracking-for-wyoming-groundwater-contamination/ |title=EPA Blames Fracking for Wyoming Groundwater Contamination |author=Susan Phillips |date=8 December 2011 |quote=federal environmental regulators have made a direct link between the controversial drilling practice known as hydraulic fracturing and groundwater contamination...The EPA found high concentrations of benzene, xylene, gasoline and diesel fuel in shallow groundwater supplies that they linked to wastewater pits. But the report also found a number of fracking chemicals in much deeper fresh water wells.|work=StateImpact Pennsylvania |publisher=WITF, WHYY & NPR |access-date=6 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="Urbina 03Aug2011">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/04/us/04natgas.html |title=A Tainted Water Well, and Concern There May be More |first=Ian |last = Urbina |date=3 August 2011 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=22 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="EPA Pavillion Dec2011">{{cite report|title=Investigation of Ground Water Contamination near Pavillion, Wyoming. Draft |first1=Dominic C. |last1=DiGiulio |first2= Richard T. |last2=Wilkin |first3= Carlyle |last3= Miller | first4=Gregory |last4 = Oberley |publisher = [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] |url=http://www.epa.gov/region8/superfund/wy/pavillion/EPA_ReportOnPavillion_Dec-8-2011.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211234805/http://www.epa.gov/region8/superfund/wy/pavillion/EPA_ReportOnPavillion_Dec-8-2011.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 11, 2011 |date=December 2011 |access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref><ref name="AutoZV-21">{{cite web |url=http://switchboard.nrdc.org/blogs/amall/incidents_where_hydraulic_frac.html |last=Mall |first=Amy |work=Switchboard: NRDC Staff Blog |publisher=[[Natural Resources Defense Council]] |title=Incidents where hydraulic fracturing is a suspected cause of drinking water contamination |date=19 December 2011 |access-date=23 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222025433/http://switchboard.nrdc.org/blogs/amall/incidents_where_hydraulic_frac.html |archive-date=22 February 2012 }}</ref>

During an event with youth environmental leaders at [[Howard University]], Jackson was asked by students about the controversial proposed [[Keystone Pipeline]], she said that "To me, it's awesome; it's awesome that we're having this conversation in this country. This should be a moment where we're having a big conversation."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.politico.com/story/2011/10/jackson-keystone-convo-awesome-067001 | title =Lisa Jackson: Keystone pipeline conversation is 'awesome' | publisher =politico.com | date = October 27, 2011  | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref> She also urged caution on the proposed project saying that "This isn't a little tiny pipeline; this is a pipeline that cuts our country literally in half."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-pipeline-epa-idUSTRE79Q60U20111027 | title =EPA says to comment soon on Keystone XL pipeline | publisher =reuters.com | date =October 27, 2011 | access-date =December 29, 2012}}</ref>

Jackson spoke out against the Senate Joint Resolution 26 (the Murkowski Amendment), which would take away the EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]], which was expanded by the 2007 Supreme Court decision in [[Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.opencongress.org/bill/111-sj26/show | title = S.J.Res.26 - A joint resolution disapproving a rule submitted by the EPA relating to the endangerment finding and the cause or contribute findings for greenhouse gases under section 202(a) of the Clean Air Act. | publisher = opencongress.org | date = June 10, 2010 | access-date = December 28, 2012 | archive-date = November 3, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121103055448/http://www.opencongress.org/bill/111-sj26/show | url-status = dead }}</ref>  In an op-ed in the [[Huffington Post]] on the Murkowski Amendment, Jackson said that "now is not the time to take a big step backward, by doubling down on the kinds of energy and environmental policies that keep America addicted to oil."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/lisa-p-jackson/the-murkowski-resolution_b_602793.html | title = The Murkowski Resolution: A Step Backward for American Clean Energy | publisher = huffingtonpost.com | author = Lisa P. Jackson | date =June 7, 2010 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}</ref> Jackson has argued against claims by lobbying groups and members of congress that the EPA is responsible for a "train wreck" of new clean air regulations and the effect of existing EPA regulations on the economy. Jackson said that "Big polluters are lobbying Congress for loopholes to use our air and water as dumping grounds. The result won't be more jobs; it will be more mercury in our air and water and more health threats to our kids."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/lisa-p-jackson/republicans-epa_b_943972.html | title =Telling the Truth About the Environment and Our Economy | publisher = huffingtonpost.com | author = Lisa P. Jackson | date =August 31, 2011 | access-date = December 28, 2012}}</ref> (For her part, Senator [[Lisa Murkowski]], the author of the amendment, argued that the regulations risked damaging the American economy.)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.murkowski.senate.gov/public/index.cfm?p=PressReleases&ContentRecord_id=00a8c969-13ab-405f-8430-e4b627cf61f3&ContentType_id=b94acc28-404a-4fc6-b143-a9e15bf92da4&Group_id=c01df158-d935-4d7a-895d-f694ddf41624&MonthDisplay=6&YearDisplay=2010|title=Sen. Murkowski: Public Deserved Vote on EPA Climate Regulations|date=June 10, 2010|publisher=murkowsi.senate.gov|access-date=December 29, 2012}}</ref>

During her tenure as head of the EPA, Jackson received criticism from the [[coal industry]] and Republican members of the House and Senate, most notably Oklahoma senator [[Jim Inhofe]], for claims of the EPA overreaching on regulating [[toxins]] released from [[coal ash]] and [[power plant]] [[Mercury (element)#Toxicity and safety|mercury emissions]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.politico.com/story/2010/10/epas-jackson-swings-back-at-critics-043168 | title = The Environmental Protection Agency's Lisa Jackson swings back at critics |publisher = politico.com | date =October 6, 2010 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}</ref> Senator Inhofe, at the time a ranking member on the [[United States Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works|Senate Committee on the Environment]] who did not believe that human activity causes global climate change,<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2009/may/05/inhofe-black-carbon-bill "US climate change denier James Inhofe joins Al Gore in fight against soot" Suzanne Goldenberg, The Guardian,5 May 2009]</ref> called on Jackson to reconsider new greenhouse gas regulations after the [[Climatic Research Unit email controversy]].<ref>{{cite news | url= https://www.nytimes.com/gwire/2010/02/23/23greenwire-epa-chief-goes-toe-to-toe-with-senate-gop-over-72892.html | title =nytimes.com | publisher = EPA Chief Goes Toe-To-Toe With Senate GOP Over Climate Science | date = February 23, 2010| access-date = December 28, 2012 | first=Robin | last=Bravender}}</ref> With Jackson responding saying that "The science behind [[climate change]] is settled, and human activity is responsible for [[global warming]]," and that "That conclusion is not a partisan one."<ref>{{cite news | url=http://content.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,1967585,00.html | title =EPA Prepares to Take the Lead on Regulating CO<sub>2</sub> | publisher = [[Time (magazine)|Time]] | date =February 23, 2010 | access-date =December 28, 2012}}</ref> Though Jackson and Inhofe have conflicted views on Environmental issues, in an interview he called her "One of my favorite Liberals."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/108862-sen-inhofe-tells-msnbcs-maddow-shes-one-of-his-three-favorite-liberals/ | title =Sen. Inhofe tells MSNBC's Maddow she's one of his 'three favorite liberals' | publisher = thehill.com | date =March 16, 2012 | access-date = December 28, 2012}}</ref>

On December 13, 2012, the assistant inspector general notified the EPA they would be conducting an audit into recordkeeping practices associated with the use of private email accounts by Jackson under the name of "Richard Windsor." The Justice Department agreed to release 12,000 emails at a rate of 3,000 per week from this account beginning January 14, 2013, in response to a lawsuit brought by a Washington attorney.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=EPA's Lisa Jackson resigning as secondary email investigation begins| author=Joel Gehrke|url=http://washingtonexaminer.com/epas-lisa-jackson-resigning-as-secondary-email-investigation-begins/article/2516938|magazine=Washington Examiner|date=27 December 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite report|title=Audit of Certain EPA Electronic Records Management Practices, Project No. OA-FY13-0113|url=http://www.epa.gov/oig/reports/notificationMemos/newStarts_12-13-2012_Audit_of_Records_Managements_Practices.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118022406/http://www.epa.gov/oig/reports/notificationMemos/newStarts_12-13-2012_Audit_of_Records_Managements_Practices.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Attorney claims EPA chief resigned over alias email accounts|author=Judson Berger|publisher=Fox News|date=27 December 2012|url= https://www.foxnews.com/politics/attorney-claims-epa-chief-resigned-over-alias-email-accounts/}}</ref>

On December 27, 2012, Jackson announced that she would be stepping down from her position as EPA administrator.<ref>{{cite news|last=Broder|first=John M.|title=E.P.A. Chief to Step Down, With Climate Still Low Priority|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/12/28/science/earth/lisa-p-jackson-of-epa-to-step-down.html?pagewanted=all|newspaper=The New York Times|date=December 27, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/2012/12/27/politics/epa-administrator-resignation/index.html?hpt=hp_t3 | work=CNN | title=EPA administrator announces resignation - CNN.com | date=December 27, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://times247.com/articles/jackson-resigned-as-epa-email-scandal-loomed | title=Integrators in Dallas Texas}}</ref>  According to the [[New York Post]], Jackson submitted her resignation because she believed that the Obama administration would move to support the Keystone pipeline and she did not want this to occur on her watch.<ref>Josh Margolin (2 January 2013), [http://www.nypost.com/p/news/national/exit_of_epa_boss_protest_9t4e0tKdNgiYPVoCgt1nBP Exit of EPA boss a protest] ''[[New York Post]]''</ref> Jackson left office on February 15, 2013, and was succeeded by Deputy Administrator [[Bob Perciasepe]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://grist.org/news/meet-bob-perciasepe-acting-epa-administrator/ | title =Meet Bob Perciasepe, acting EPA administrator | publisher =grist.org | author =Phillip Bump | date =February 15, 2013 | access-date =February 18, 2013}}</ref>

At a House hearing in September 2013, Jackson denied knowledge of any government secrecy and denied that she tried to evade federal recordkeeping laws.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dinan|first=Stephan|title=Ex-EPA chief Lisa Jackson denies trying to avoid sunshine laws|url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2013/sep/10/ex-epa-chief-lisa-jackson-denies-trying-avoid-suns/|newspaper=Washington Times|access-date=10 September 2013}}</ref>

==Tenure at Apple==
In 2013, Jackson became [[Apple Inc.]]'s vice president of environment, policy and social initiatives, reporting to CEO [[Tim Cook]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://investor.apple.com/leadership-and-governance/person-details/default.aspx?ItemId=43c7ad59-5aa4-49ab-b131-87d3b55046b7 | title=Leadership and Governance – Person Details – Apple }}</ref> Apple announced in December 2025 that she would retire in January 2026.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/12/apple-announces-executive-transitions/?1764883861 | title=Apple announces executive transitions }}</ref> In February 2026, [[Conservation International]] named Jackson interim chair of its board of directors.<ref name="PRNewswire-CI-NewLeadership-2026">{{cite news |title=Conservation International Announces New CEO and New Interim Chairman of the Board to Lead Global Progress on Nature Conservation for People |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/apac/news-releases/conservation-international-announces-new-ceo-and-new-interim-chairman-of-the-board-to-lead-global-progress-on-nature-conservation-for-people-302682912.html |website=PR Newswire |date=February 11, 2026}}</ref>
